<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is a Godot Engine 4 C++ module/extension that provides a robust voxel system for generating, editing, and rendering 3D volumetric terrains. The module integrates deep into Godot (with editor plugins, runtime voxel engine code, and GDExtension support) and covers a large range of functionality—from voxel storage and streaming to generation algorithms, meshing, modifiers, and specialized terrain types (both blocky and smooth). Here’s how you can create an accurate and detailed system design diagram for this project:

1. Define the Major Components and Their Roles:
   • Voxel Engine Core: Central runtime logic (see directories like engine/voxel_engine.cpp, engine/voxel_engine_gd.cpp, and engine/voxel_engine_updater.cpp). This is the heart of voxel processing.
   • Voxel Data Storage and Streaming: Components that handle voxel data management (storage/ and streams/ directories, including voxel_buffer, voxel_data, region files, SQLite streams, etc.).
   • Voxel Generators: Components responsible for creating voxel data procedurally (generators/ directory with subfolders for simple algorithms, graph-based generators, and multipass generators).
   • Voxel Meshers: Responsible for converting voxel data into meshes, both blocky and smooth (meshers/ directory subdivided into blocky, cubes, and transvoxel approaches).
   • Voxel Modifiers: Modules that alter voxel data (modifiers/, with further support for Godot integration).
   • Editor Integration and Tools: Modules that add custom editor features and debugging tools (editor/ directory, including graph editors, library inspectors, instance modules, and custom dialogs).
   • Shader Management: Shader scripts and shader generation for rendering details (shaders/ directory, including development shader templates and production shader code).
   • Third-party Dependencies: Libraries such as FastNoise, Meshoptimizer, lz4, and SQLite are included to enhance noise generation, mesh optimization, and data persistence.

2. Identify Relationships and Data Flow:
   • At the “top” you have Godot itself interfacing with the Voxel Tools via GDExtension.
   • The Voxel Engine Core communicates with the Voxel Generators to create terrain data. Data flows from generators into the storage/streams layers, where voxel data is buffered, saved/loaded, and possibly streamed.
   • The Meshers then take this voxel data to generate chunked meshes, which are then passed to the rendering pipeline (supported by shaders).
   • Voxel Modifiers and the Voxel Graph system allow further dynamic modifications to the voxel data at runtime.
   • Editor Components facilitate design-time tweaking, visualization, and debugging. They connect to most of the runtime components (engine, generators, meshers) and also offer enhancements like inspector plugins, node dialogs, and custom Godot editor windows.

3. Emphasize Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • Modular design and separation of concerns: Each folder (engine, generators, meshers, modifiers, and streams) represents a distinct module/component.
   • Integration with Godot via GDExtension: Highlight the two-way interface between the native C++ modules and Godot’s scripting layer (exposed via project/addons and project/voxel.gdextension files).
   • Use of third-party libraries, such as FastNoise (for procedural generation) and Meshoptimizer (for mesh simplification and performance), which play key roles in generating and processing data.

4. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Identify and label each major component clearly within the diagram.
   • Use directional arrows to indicate the flow: for instance, show how user input or runtime events trigger the Voxel Engine, which in turn queries the appropriate generator, passes data to the storage/stream layer, and orchestrates mesher and modifier operations.
   • Differentiate components with shapes or colors (for example, use one color for runtime modules like the engine, another for tools/editor integrations, and yet another for external libraries or utility functions).
   • Include sub-components as needed: for example, under Voxel Generators, you might show a branch for “Graph-based Generators” (from generators/graph) versus “Simple Generators” (from generators/simple).
   • Clearly indicate integration points with Godot (e.g., editor plugins, GDExtension interfaces) so that the interaction between native code and Godot’s editor/runtime is transparent.
   • Don’t forget to mark the persistence and streaming subsystem (storage and streams) to show how data flows from generation to disk/network and eventually to the meshers.

5. Tips for Detailed Diagram Construction:
   • Start with high-level components and then “zoom in” on each if necessary; use nested diagrams or layered views.
   • Ensure each component’s responsibilities (e.g., procedural generation, meshing, storage) are labeled alongside any major libraries or dependencies employed.
   • For each module, include key configuration items—for instance, the workflows, SConstruct, and build configuration files show the build and CI pipelines supporting the project.
   • It’s beneficial to annotate interactions and dependencies, for example, noting that the Voxel Engine Updater coordinates tasks between streaming, generation, and editing.
   • Use sparing yet descriptive text within the diagram for clarity.

Using these guidelines, you can produce a system design diagram that fully captures:
   - The core engine and its integration with Godot via GDExtension.
   - The modular nature of the voxel generation, meshing, and modification subsystems.
   - The data flow from voxel generation to storage, then to mesh generation and rendering.
   - The editor integration that enhances usability and debugging.

This comprehensive diagram will help any principal software engineer quickly understand the modular structure and detailed interactions that make up the Voxel Tools for Godot, and it will serve as an excellent resource for onboarding new contributors or guiding technical enhancements.
</explanation>
